title: THE PROPHECY HIDDEN IN PASSOVER
paragraphs: THE PROPHECY HIDDEN IN PASSOVER
The night began with a meal.
Not a sermon.
Not a miracle.
Not a battle.
A meal.

Families gathered around tables. Children asked questions. Lamb was eaten. Bitter herbs burned the tongue. Unleavened bread cracked between trembling hands. Candles flickered against walls while stories older than memory filled the room.
To many, Passover is simply the story of Israel's liberation from Egypt.
But hidden within that sacred night is one of the most breathtaking prophetic revelations in all of Scripture.
A prophecy so precise, so layered, so astonishingly detailed that once it is seen, it becomes impossible to unsee.
Passover was never merely about Egypt.
It was always about Jesus.
Long before Bethlehem.
Long before Calvary.
Long before the empty tomb.
The Gospel was already sitting at the table.
The story begins in slavery.

Israel had been trapped in Egypt for generations. What began as refuge during Joseph's lifetime became oppression under Pharaoh. The people cried out to God, and God raised up Moses as their deliverer.
Then came the plagues.
Blood.
Frogs.
Gnats.
Flies.
Disease.
Boils.
Hail.
Locusts.
Darkness.
Nine judgments fell upon Egypt, yet Pharaoh's heart remained hard.
Then came the tenth.
The final plague.
Death would pass through the land.
Every firstborn son would die.
But God provided a way of escape.
In Exodus 12, the Lord instructed every household to take a lamb without blemish.
The Hebrew phrase is "seh tamim" (שֶׂה תָמִים), meaning a flawless, complete, unblemished lamb.
This was no random detail.
The sacrifice had to be perfect.
The lamb would be examined.
Tested.
Inspected.
Then killed.
Its blood would be placed on the doorposts and lintel of the home.
When judgment came, God declared:
"When I see the blood, I will pass over you" (Exodus 12:13).
Notice carefully.
The people were not saved because they were morally superior.
They were not spared because they were Israelites.
They were not protected because of good works.
They were protected because of the blood.
The blood stood between them and judgment.
Thousands of years later, another Lamb would stand between humanity and judgment.
This is where the prophecy begins to emerge.
The Hebrew word for Passover is "Pesach" (פֶּסַח).
It means to pass over, spare, or protect.
Every year Israel celebrated Pesach to remember deliverance from Egypt.
Yet every celebration pointed beyond itself.
The feast was a shadow.
The substance was coming.
When John the Baptist saw Jesus approaching the Jordan River, he did not call Him a teacher.
He did not call Him a prophet.
He did not call Him a revolutionary.
He declared:
"Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world" (John 1:29).
To first-century Jewish ears, this statement was explosive.
Lamb.
Passover.
Sacrifice.
Deliverance.
Blood.
Redemption.
John was announcing that the true Passover Lamb had finally arrived.
What Egypt foreshadowed, Christ would fulfill.
What animal blood symbolized, Christ's blood would accomplish.
What Passover predicted, Jesus embodied.
The parallels become even more astonishing.
The Passover lamb had to be without blemish.
Jesus lived a sinless life.
The Passover lamb was examined before sacrifice.
Jesus was examined by religious leaders, Pilate, Herod, and Roman authorities.
No legitimate fault could be found in Him.
Pilate himself declared:
"I find no guilt in Him."
The Passover lamb was sacrificed.
Jesus was crucified.
The blood of the lamb protected households from judgment.
The blood of Christ protects believers from eternal judgment.
The Passover lamb brought temporary deliverance from physical death.
Jesus brings eternal deliverance from spiritual death.
None of this happened by accident.
The Apostle Paul writes:
The Greek text is even more direct.
"Pascha hēmōn etythē Christos."
"Our Passover has been sacrificed—Christ."
Paul leaves no ambiguity.
Jesus is the fulfillment of Passover.
Yet the prophecy goes even deeper.
According to Exodus 12:3, the lamb was selected on the tenth day of the month Nisan.
It was then kept under observation until the fourteenth day when it was sacrificed.
For four days the lamb was examined.
Observed.
Inspected.
Jesus entered Jerusalem during the very season when Passover lambs were being selected.
As He entered the city, crowds shouted:
"Hosanna!"
They waved palm branches and welcomed Him as King.
What many did not realize was that God's Lamb was entering Jerusalem at the same time the Passover lambs were being chosen.
Then came days of questioning.
Religious leaders challenged Him.
Lawyers tested Him.
Pharisees interrogated Him.
Sadducees attempted to trap Him.
Every examination only confirmed His perfection.
The Lamb was spotless.
The Lamb was ready.
Then came the crucifixion.
The timing is staggering.
Ancient Jewish historian Josephus records that vast numbers of lambs were slaughtered during Passover in Jerusalem.
As priests prepared sacrifices throughout the city, Jesus hung upon a cross outside its walls.
The shadow and the reality met.
The symbol and the fulfillment collided.
The Lamb of God was being offered.
At the exact moment humanity needed Him most.
Yet another hidden prophecy emerges from Exodus 12.
God commanded:
"Do not break any of its bones."
The Hebrew reads:
"Ve'etzem lo tishberu bo."
Not one bone was to be broken.
Centuries later Roman soldiers arrived at Golgotha.
Victims often had their legs shattered to accelerate death.
But when they came to Jesus, He was already dead.
Instead of breaking His bones, they pierced His side.
John records:
"Not one of His bones will be broken."
What appeared to be a small ceremonial detail in Passover became another astonishing prophetic marker fulfilled in Christ.
The precision is breathtaking.
The God who authored Exodus also authored redemption.
Nothing was random.
Nothing was accidental.
Nothing escaped divine design.
Then there is the unleavened bread.
Throughout Scripture, leaven often symbolizes sin and corruption.
Passover required bread without leaven.
Pure.
Uncontaminated.
The Hebrew word is "matzah" (מַצָּה).
Unleavened bread.
Jesus identified Himself as the Bread of Life.
Unlike fallen humanity, He was untouched by sin.
The unleavened bread of Passover pointed toward the sinless Messiah.
Even the cup tells a story.
At the Last Supper, celebrated during Passover, Jesus took the cup and declared:
"This cup is the new covenant in My blood."
The meal suddenly transformed.
The symbols became personal.
The Lamb sat at the table.
The sacrifice held the cup.
The fulfillment interpreted the prophecy.
The Deliverer explained deliverance.
Every piece pointed to Him.
Every shadow found its substance.
Every prophecy found its fulfillment.
Yet perhaps the most powerful part of Passover is not historical.
It is personal.
Because Egypt is not merely a location.
It is a picture.
A picture of bondage.
Addiction.
Fear.
Pride.
Shame.
Brokenness.
Sin.
Many people live exactly where Israel once lived.
Trapped.
Exhausted.
Powerless.
Unable to free themselves.
Trying harder.
Failing again.
Carrying chains nobody else sees.
But the message of Passover remains unchanged.
God still provides a Lamb.
The Gospel is not advice.
It is rescue.
Jesus did not come merely to improve humanity.
He came to save humanity.
The blood on the doorposts was not symbolic sentiment.
It was the difference between life and death.
Likewise, the cross is not a religious decoration.
It is the dividing line between condemnation and redemption.
This is why grace is so scandalous.
The Israelites were not spared because they earned it.
Believers are not saved because they deserve it.
Grace has always offended human pride.
Because grace announces that salvation belongs entirely to God.
The cross exposes our inability.
The resurrection reveals His power.
And together they tell the greatest story ever told.
The story of a God who stepped into human history to save people who could never save themselves.
This is the prophecy hidden in Passover.
Not merely a feast.
Not merely a Jewish tradition.
Not merely an ancient remembrance.
It is the Gospel concealed in Exodus and revealed in Christ.
It is God's redemption story written centuries before Calvary.
It is the Lamb hidden in the shadows until the fullness of time arrived.
And perhaps the most astonishing truth of all is this:
The blood that once covered doorposts now covers lives.
The Lamb who was slain still saves.
The Deliverer still rescues.
The chains still break.
The graves still open.
The lost still come home.
Maybe that is why this story continues to move hearts after thousands of years.
Because every human soul knows what it feels like to need deliverance.
Every heart knows what it feels like to need mercy.
Every life carries evidence of Egypt somewhere.
And every person desperately needs a Lamb.
If this message stirred something deep within you, do not keep it to yourself.
What "Egypt" has God delivered you from—or what are you still asking Him to deliver you from?
Your testimony may become someone else's breakthrough.
The Lamb was never the end of the story—it was God's way of revealing the Author.
